title: Psalm 136: His Loving Devotion Endures Forever
summary: In twenty-six lines, each answered by the same refrain, Israel gives thanks to the LORD as the God of gods and Lord of lords. The psalm moves from creation to the exodus, the wilderness, the defeat of Sihon and Og, and the gift of the land, then to God's care for his people in their low estate and his provision of food for every creature. After every act comes the same answer: his loving devotion endures forever.
story: Psalm 136 follows Psalm 135 closely, retelling much of the same history (the firstborn of Egypt, Sihon and Og, the land given as an inheritance) but turning proclamation into thanksgiving. Where Psalm 135 argued against idols, Psalm 136 simply gives thanks, line after line. It stands near the end of Book V of the Psalter, and it is followed immediately by Psalm 137, the lament by the rivers of Babylon. The placement is telling: a psalm that says God's loving devotion never ends sits beside a psalm sung by people who have lost their city, their temple, and their songs. The Psalter does not let either one silence the other.
historical:
The psalm has no superscription. Its refrain, give thanks to the LORD, for he is good, his loving devotion endures forever, was one of Israel's best known liturgical responses. The historical books place it at great moments of worship: when David brought the ark to Jerusalem (1 Chronicles 16:34, 41), when Solomon dedicated the temple (2 Chronicles 5:13 and 7:3), when Jehoshaphat's singers went out before the army (2 Chronicles 20:21), and when the returned exiles laid the foundation of the Second Temple (Ezra 3:11). Jeremiah also foresaw the words being sung again in the restored land (Jeremiah 33:11). The psalm itself may be later than some of these occasions, but it preserves a response that was sung over many centuries.

In later Jewish tradition Psalm 136 came to be called the Great Hallel (the great praise), distinct from the Egyptian Hallel of Psalms 113 to 118 sung at Passover. It has long been used at Passover and on festivals, fitting for a psalm that retells the exodus.
cultural:
The refrain gives the psalm its form, and that form points to how it was sung. A leader, perhaps a Levite singer, would call out the first half of each verse, and the congregation would answer with the refrain. Even people who could not read and did not know the whole psalm could take part. This kind of call and response was common in Israel's worship (compare Ezra 3:11, where the people answer the singers).

The titles in verses 2 and 3, God of gods and Lord of lords, used the language of an ancient world full of gods and kings. Every nation had its pantheon, and great kings claimed titles like king of kings. The psalm does not argue about whether the other gods exist; it simply declares that the LORD is supreme over whatever power anyone else might worship. The phrase “with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm” (verse 12) is the stock language of Deuteronomy for the exodus (Deuteronomy 4:34 and 26:8), and it may have been chosen partly because Egyptian royal propaganda loved to picture Pharaoh's own strong arm.
literary: Psalm 136 is a litany, and its structure is easy to hear. Verses 1 to 3 open with a threefold call to give thanks, and verse 26 closes with the same call, framing the whole. Verses 4 to 9 praise God as Creator, following the order of Genesis 1 from the heavens to the lights of day and night. Verses 10 to 22 praise him as Redeemer: the plague on the firstborn, the exodus, the crossing of the Red Sea, the wilderness, and the victory over kings that led to the gift of the land. Verses 23 to 25 bring the story into the present tense, with God remembering us in our low estate and giving food to every creature. Every verse ends with the same line, twenty-six times. The repetition is the point: whatever God does, whether he makes stars, parts a sea, or feeds an animal, it comes from the same steady love.

outline.t: Give thanks to the God of gods and Lord of lords
The Creator of heavens, earth, and lights
The exodus, the sea, and the wilderness
Kings struck down and the land given
Remembered in our low estate, fed with every creature
Give thanks to the God of heaven

doctrines.note: The refrain makes God's steadfast love the constant beneath every act. His power in creation and his judgment on Pharaoh are not in tension with his love; the psalm treats all of them as expressions of the same faithful character.

God made the heavens by his understanding, spread out the earth, and set the sun and moon to rule day and night. Creation is the first of his acts of loving devotion, not a neutral stage for the real story.
The same God who divided the sea gives food to every creature. The psalm holds the spectacular and the ordinary together, so that daily bread is seen as the same kind of gift as the exodus.

words.note: Chesed, loving devotion, often translated steadfast love, mercy, or loyal love. It describes faithful kindness within a relationship, loyalty that goes beyond what is strictly owed and keeps going. It appears in every one of the psalm's twenty-six verses. The psalm teaches the meaning of the word by showing it at work in creation, rescue, and daily provision.

Olam, forever or long duration. The word can mean a very long time, into the distant past or future, and it often means for all time. Paired with chesed in the refrain, it says that God's love is not a mood or a season. It outlasts every change the psalm describes, from Egypt to the land to the present day.

Yadah, to give thanks. The verb means to acknowledge or confess publicly, and in worship it means to thank God by declaring what he has done. That is why the psalm is a list of his acts: in Israel, giving thanks meant telling the story out loud, in front of others.

Shephel, low estate or humiliation. The word appears only here and in Ecclesiastes 10:6. Verse 23 uses it to bring the ancient story into the worshipers' own lives: the God who acted in Egypt also remembered us when we were brought low, which may refer to the exile and its aftermath.

christ: The psalm's refrain, that God's loving devotion endures forever, finds its fullest expression in the New Testament's account of Christ. John writes that the Word became flesh, full of grace and truth (John 1:14), words that many scholars hear as a Greek echo of the Old Testament pair steadfast love and faithfulness. The psalm moves from creation to redemption to daily provision, and the New Testament names Christ as the one through whom all things were made (John 1:3), the one who accomplished a new exodus in his death and resurrection (Luke 9:31 uses the Greek word exodus for his departure at Jerusalem), and the one who taught his disciples to ask for daily bread. On the night he was betrayed, Jesus and his disciples sang a hymn after the Passover meal (Matthew 26:30); that hymn is usually identified with the Egyptian Hallel, Psalms 113 to 118, rather than this psalm, but it shows Jesus praying Israel's festival songs of thanksgiving on the way to the cross.

hard.q: How can a psalm give thanks for God's love in the same breath as the death of Egypt's firstborn and the slaughter of kings?
hard.a: Verses 10, 15, and 17 to 20 set the refrain of loving devotion after acts of judgment, and it can sound as though the psalm celebrates death. The psalm is telling the story from the viewpoint of a people who were slaves and were set free. For Israel, the judgment on Pharaoh and the defeat of kings who came out to destroy them were the form God's love took toward them: they were rescued from oppressors who would not let them go. The Old Testament is also clear that God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked (Ezekiel 18:23), and the exodus account presents the plagues as the end of a long refusal by Pharaoh. Readers differ on how to hold these texts together. Some stress that God's love for the oppressed necessarily includes opposition to the oppressor; others emphasize that these were particular acts in Israel's founding history, not a pattern for all wars. The psalm's refrain claims that even judgment serves the purposes of a love that endures.

questions: The psalm places creation, national rescue, and daily food side by side as acts of the same love. Which of these do you find easiest to thank God for, and which do you tend to overlook?
If you wrote your own version of this psalm, what acts of God in your life would you list before each refrain?
Repetition can become empty, or it can carve something deep. How might repeating a single truth over and over shape the way a person sees their life?
